title: United Airlines 266

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report: United Airlines Flight 266, Boeing 727-22C

summary: United Airlines Flight 266 crashed into Santa Monica Bay four minutes after takeoff from Los Angeles International Airport. The No. 3 generator had been non-functional and was masked with tape before flight, masked by improper maintenance procedures. After engine No. 1 fire warning and shutdown, the No. 2 generator also failed resulting in total loss of electrical power. Flying at night in instrument conditions without attitude instruments, the crew became spatially disoriented and lost control of the aircraft. All 38 aboard were killed.
probable_cause: The probable cause of this accident was loss of attitude orientation during a night, instrument departure in which all attitude instruments were disabled by loss of electrical power. The Board has been unable to determine why all generator power was lost or why the standby electrical power system either was not activated or failed to function. (p. 4, 33)

factors.evidence: Fire warning activated on engine No. 1 approximately 2 minutes after takeoff during climb to departure control; crew shut down engine No. 1 and reported loss of all functioning generators (p. 5, 21)
Loss of all electrical power forced manual control of aircraft in night instrument conditions; standby electrical system either was not activated or failed to function (p. 32)
Crew was without reliable attitude reference from point No. 2 generator was lost until impact; flying at night in instrument conditions, pilots quickly became spatially disoriented (p. 21, 32)
Aircraft crashed into Santa Monica Bay at steep nose-down angle with right wing low attitude; crew lost control due to spatial disorientation and loss of attitude reference instruments (p. 19-20)

events.text: United Flight 266, Boeing 727-22C N4724U, departs Runway 25L at Los Angeles International Airport for flight to Milwaukee in night instrument conditions (p. 5)
Engine No. 1 fire warning activated approximately 2 minutes after takeoff during climb; crew reports fire warning to Departure Control and requests return to airport (p. 4, 21)
Crew shuts down engine No. 1 and reports loss of all functioning generators to Departure Control (p. 5)
No. 2 generator ceases operating after becoming sole power source; all electrical power is lost; attitude instruments and lights go dark (p. 19)
With loss of all electrical power, pilots lose attitude reference; without attitude indicators, crew becomes spatially disoriented flying at night in instrument conditions (p. 19, 32)
First officer exclaims during final moments: Keep it going up - you're a thousand feet - pull it up (p. 20)
Aircraft crashes into Pacific Ocean at steep nose-down angle, right wing low attitude; aircraft destroyed on impact; wreckage scattered (p. 19-20)
All 38 aboard killed (6 crew members and 32 passengers); aircraft destroyed; limited wreckage scatter and fragmentation pattern indicate high-speed impact (p. 4-5, 19)

cvr.speaker: FO
cvr.text: Keep it going up - you're a thousand feet - pull it up

recommendations.text: Make automatic switching of essential power to standby power upon loss of all generators a mandatory requirement for all turbine-powered aircraft (p. 33)

Until automatic switching can be implemented, require emergency checklists for all airlines for Loss of All Generators procedure to ensure second officer or captain immediately switches essential power to standby or emergency position (p. 33)
Provide positive indication to second officer on Boeing 727 panel when standby system is being powered from battery, such as illuminating light when standby system is activated (p. 34)
Consider transfer of standby feature from essential power selector switch to separate ON-OFF toggle switch for improved accessibility (p. 34)

safety_changes: Automatic standby power activation systems required on large transport aircraft
Boeing 727 emergency procedure revisions implemented requiring manual standby power switching
Installation of third independent attitude indicator on large turbojet aircraft
Enhanced redundancy requirements for electrical power systems in aircraft design
